voyage.name: GPO Museum
voyage.content: The GPO is the headquarters of the Post Office in Ireland, built in Neo-Classical style 1814-1818. In 1916 it was occupied by Irish rebels led by PH Pearse, who read the Proclamation of the Republic outside the front door of the building. The interior was burnt out by shelling from government forces against the rebels, but the exterior survived. Subsequently the GPO was restored, reopening in 1929, and remains a busy

voyage.name: St Mary's Pro-Cathedral
voyage.content: Dublin's Catholic cathedral, built in 1825. Catholicism was always the majority religion in Ireland, but its practice was forbidden until the 19th century. The official cathedral is Christ Church, so designated by the Pope in 1300, but taken over by the Protestants in the 16th century. When the laws relaxed, St Mary's was built in neo-Classical style as a temporary or "pro"-cathedral, until such time as the Pope decr

voyage.name: National Leprechaun Museum
voyage.content: The "little folk" appeared in lore around 1300 AD but only flourished from the 19th century Celtic revival, dressed in late Georgian garb in an idealised rural past, mending a shoe. They proliferated into the silliest of 20th century Irish tourism, like greenfly upon the Rose of Tralee, and fell out of fashion. This museum is immersive telling of the stories woven around them, with a daytime and darker night show.

voyage.name: Hugh Lane Gallery
voyage.address: Charlemont House, Parnell Square North D01 F2X9
voyage.content: Sir Hugh Lane (1875-1915) was one of the first collectors of modern art. He died in the sinking of Lusitania and this public gallery reflects his Will, which involved about as much negotiation, fudge and compromise as the Treaty for Irish independence. The permanent exhibitions are mostly contemporary Irish artists, plus Francis Bacon's studio, relocated from London in 2001. Charlemont House was built in 1763 and in

voyage.name: James Joyce Centre
voyage.address: 35 North Great George's St D01 WK44
voyage.content: Georgian townhouse with an exhibition of Joyce's life and times. He never lived here himself.

voyage.name: EPIC The Irish Emigration Museum
voyage.price: Adult €21, child 6-12 €10.50, teen 13-17 €14.50, under 5s free, senior €19
voyage.address: CHQ, Custom House Quay D01 R9Y0
voyage.content: Over the centuries more than 10 million people emigrated from Ireland; this is the story of why they left, where they went and how they shaped the world.

voyage.name: The Jeanie Johnston
voyage.content: One million Irish people fled Ireland during the famine. 2500 took a gruelling voyage aboard the Jeanie Johnston, and this is a replica. You take a 50 min tour above and below deck.

voyage.name: Green on Red Gallery
voyage.address: Park Lane, Spencer Dock D01 Y821
voyage.content: Commercial gallery exhibiting Irish and international modern art.

voyage.name: Outhouse LGBTQ+ Centre
voyage.content: Safe space for LGBTQ+ people, with community café, social and cultural events, resources and support services, a queer library, theatre and meeting spaces.

voyage.name: 14 Henrietta Street
voyage.content: Many Dubliners lived in buildings like this. Built in the 1740s, its first occupant was Lord Viscount Molesworth and his family, and after him came a series of Right Honorable This and Viscount That and Bishop of Wherever. But the union with England in 1801 drained power and money to London, and the neighbourhood went downhill. Rural folk flocked to Dublin after the famine, so the building was broken up into tenement

voyage.name: Trinity College
voyage.hours: Kells: May-Sep Mon-Sat 8:30AM-7PM, Sun 9:30AM-5PM; Oct-Apr Mon-Sat 9:30AM-5PM, Sun noon-4:30PM
voyage.content: Trinity College is the fine Georgian campus of the University of Dublin. It's generally open to stroll around in daylight hours, but it is a working university, and most interiors are off-limits to tourists. You can visit the Chapel near the front (west) gate of the College. But the big attraction is the Old Library and Book of Kells. Book online, otherwise buy your ticket from the machines under the Lecky library ju

voyage.name: Irish Whiskey Museum
voyage.content: And not before time. Irish distilleries have for too long pumped out bland commercial fare, though the country has all the ingredients and know-how to produce whiskey of character to rival single-malt Scotch.

voyage.name: National Gallery of Ireland
voyage.hours: Tue Wed Fri Sat 9:15AM-5:30PM, Thu 9:15AM-8:30PM, Sun Mon 11AM-5:30PM
voyage.content: Impressive national collection of Irish and European Art. In January the gallery displays its watercolours by JMW Turner; the original donor specified that they had to be kept out of the light for the rest of the year.

voyage.name: National Museum of Ireland - Archaeology
voyage.content: Amazing display of Ireland's artefacts from prehistory through the Viking era to independence. The standout is the Treasury (with the 12th century Ardagh Chalice and 9th century Tara Brooch), and the prehistoric jewellery: gold and silver beautifully worked and carved.

voyage.name: Leinster House
voyage.content: This opulent Georgian mansion is in the same block as the Archaeology Museum. Designed by Cassels, it was built in 1745 as the residence of the Duke of Leinster at a time when the southside was unfashionable. It proved an "anchor development" and Dublin's centre of power and culture soon gravitated from the northside. From 1922 it became the temporary base of the Oireachtas, the Irish bi-cameral parliament, and like

voyage.name: National Museum of Ireland - Natural History
voyage.hours: closed for refurbishment as of April 2026, but some of the collections are on display in the Dead Zoo Lab at their Collins Barracks site
voyage.content: The "Dead Zoo" contains a comprehensive zoological collection presented in a manner unchanged since its establishment in Victorian times.

voyage.name: Little Museum of Dublin
voyage.content: Their main building on St Stephen's Green is closed for renovation, so this is a temporary home. It displays the 20th-century social, cultural and political history of Dublin city, with many artefacts donated by Dubliners. Visit by guided tour every hour.

voyage.name: Irish Jewish Museum
voyage.content: Exhibiting Jewish life in the cities - as in Great Britain, many were emigres from "White Russia". Their best known member is fictional, Leopold Bloom the protagonist of Ulysses.

voyage.name: Dublin Castle
voyage.content: Former seat of British rule in Ireland. The guided tour takes in the medieval basements and Chapel Royal, then you see the State Apartments in your own time. You can skip the tour and just see the apartments for less.

voyage.name: Chester Beatty Library
voyage.hours: Mar-Oct Mon Tue Thu-Sat 10AM-5:30PM, Wed 10AM-8PM, Sun noon-5:30PM, Nov-Feb closed Mon
voyage.content: Sir Alfred Chester Beatty (1875-1968) was an American mining magnate who amassed a fabulous collection of early books and manuscripts and oriental art. He moved to London and collaborated generously with the British Museum, but in 1950 there was a falling-out and he moved to Ireland. He established the library to avoid his collection being split up; it's now in the Clock Tower in the Castle gardens.

voyage.name: Christ Church Cathedral
voyage.hours: Apr-Sep Mon-Sat 9:30AM-7PM, Sun 12:30-14:30PM & 4:30-7PM; Oct-Mar Mon-Sat 9:30AM-5PM, Sun 12:30-2:30PM
voyage.content: A wooden church was built by the Vikings around 1030, and the first stone church was from the 1180s. So this is the oldest building in Dublin, though it underwent a massive restoration in the 1870s. It became Protestant under Henty VIII, apart from a brief Roman Catholic interlude in 1690 when the exiled James II was campaigning in Ireland, and the Vatican still claims it. The oldest part is the large crypt, where am

voyage.name: Dublinia
voyage.content: Exhibition of life in the Viking settlement and medieval city, child-friendly.

voyage.name: St Patrick's Cathedral
voyage.content: Founded in 1191, it became Anglican at the Reformation, so the Protestants had two cathedrals in the same city while the Catholics had none. It feuded with Christ Church over rights and precedence, until 1871 when Christ Church was nominated the senior church for Dublin and Glendalough and St Patrick's for the rest of Ireland. Jonathan Swift, author of Gulliver's Travels, was dean of St Patrick's from 1713 to 1745 an

voyage.name: National Museum of Ireland - Decorative Arts & History
voyage.address: Collins Barracks, Benburb St D07 XKV4
voyage.content: The building is remarkable, a Georgian barracks around a parade square. Displays decorative arts and artefacts over 400 years, from rustic houses through Georgian elegance to "Proclaiming a Republic", the events of Easter 1916 when the interior decor of the Post Office took a sad turn for the worse.

voyage.name: Irish Museum of Modern Art
voyage.address: Royal Hospital, Military Road, Kilmainham D08 FW31
voyage.content: Modern and contemporary art, housed in the Royal Hospital of 1684. See also the elegant courtyard and formal gardens.

voyage.name: Kilmainham Gaol
voyage.content: This prison was in use 1796-1924; thousands have passed through, including many convicts transported to Australia. It's best known as the place where the rebels from the 1916 Easter Rising were executed. (Several now lie in Arbour Hill Cemetery just north of the Decorative Arts Museum.) Access by guided tour every 30 min, pre-booking essential.

voyage.name: Dublin Zoo
voyage.content: Opened in 1830 and extended in 1997, this Zoo has a dozen habitats and is the largest in Ireland.

voyage.name: Rathfarnham Castle
voyage.content: Built as a fortified mansion around 1583 and prettified in the 18th century, it fell derelict in the 19th but has been restored as a museum.

voyage.name: Pearse Museum
voyage.address: St Enda's Park, Rathfarnham D16 Y7Y5
voyage.content: Patrick Pearse (1879-1916) saw Irish culture and language as essential for national independence. His one and only case as a barrister was his unsuccessful defence of a Donegal tradesman for using an "illegible" sign, and the verdict effectively made Irish signage illegal. He set up a language school in 1908, which moved here in 1910. He was also a leading Republican, reading the proclamation of independence on the G

voyage.name: Glasnevin Cemetery
voyage.content: This opened as an RC cemetery in 1832, in an era when the Catholics weren't allowed their own parish churches, and their burials were begrudged affairs in Protestant ground. Glasnevin has grown and grown, expanding south across Finglas road into the St Paul's section, but the famous names are north side. You can visit the cemetery free, but to make sense of it go to the visitor centre (daily 10AM-5PM, closed M Tu in

voyage.name: National Botanic Gardens
voyage.hours: Mar-Oct Mon-Fri 9AM-5PM, Sat Sun 10AM-6PM; Nov-Feb Mon-Fri 9AM-4:30PM, Sat Sun 10AM-4:30PM
voyage.content: Extensive gardens favouring alkaline-loving species. The great Palm House was where Wittgenstein often came to warm his lugubrious backside. A gateway leads into Glasnevin Cemetery adjacent. The gardens also manage the arboretum at Kilmacurragh near Wicklow Town.

voyage.name: Guinness Storehouse
voyage.content: Guinness is brewed in 49 countries and Ireland just happens to be one of them. The St James Gate brewery is still in production, now part of Diageo, and this vast storehouse has become an exhibition (self-guided) on the drink and the Guinness family. Price of entry includes a pint at the seventh floor Gravity Bar, which forms the head of the giant pint of stout formed by the atrium. Outside, touristy-trappy horse-dra

voyage.name: Teeling Distillery
voyage.price: Tasting tour €25 (pointless going for the cheaper "cocktail" tour)
voyage.content: Distillery opened in 2015, primarily for whiskey but with small amounts of poitín.

voyage.name: Jameson Distillery
voyage.content: Jameson whiskey was produced in Dublin from 1780 to 1976, when the business relocated to Midleton near Cork. So the old Bow St distillery no longer makes whiskey but has been converted into a museum about the process and industry.

voyage.name: The Lazy Bike Tour Company
voyage.content: Two-hour bike tours of the major sights and off the beaten track, with informative guides.

voyage.name: Walking Tours
voyage.content: Dublin city is famous for its characters. A great way to experience and live the city is by learning about it from people who are characters themselves - Dublin Tour Guides. Tours can vary from one to four hours in length and include, as well as the standard sightseeing tour, tours on topics like the paranormal and ghosts, music and song, literature, historical, 1916 Rising, and even Irish mythology. There are variou

voyage.name: Dublin Literary Pub Crawl
voyage.content: This is the most ingenious crash course in Irish literature, history, architecture and pub bonhomie yet devised... It combines street theatre with the 'craic' that makes Dublin pubs the liveliest in Europe. It is a highly enjoyable evening that gives you the pleasant notion of replacing brain cells as you drown them. The tour is a kind of rough guide to the cultural, religious and political life of the city. Performa

voyage.name: Abbey Theatre
voyage.content: Opened in 1904, and always at the centre of the Irish drama scene, the Abbey is a good venue for catching local playwrights' work but with a global repertoire. It's intended to replace the current building with two new theatres fronting onto the Liffey. This will mean a lengthy closure, but the work has not started.

voyage.name: Gaiety Theatre
voyage.content: Founded in 1871 so this is the oldest continually operating theatre in Dublin. It hosts popular musical shows, opera, ballet, dance and drama.

voyage.name: Gate Theatre
voyage.content: This has a focus on European and American theatre ranging from classics to modern plays. It was established as a theatre company in 1928 by Hilton Edward and Micheál MacLiammóir.

voyage.name: National Concert Hall
voyage.content: This offers classical concerts. Frequent performances by the resident orchestra, the RTÉ National Symphony Orchestra. The main auditorium seats 1200 and there are three smaller spaces. It was built in 1865 for a trade fair then became an entertainment venue then the core of University College Dublin. It became a concert hall from 1981 when UCD moved to the Belfield campus.

voyage.name: Bord Gáis Energy Theatre
voyage.content: The theatre offers a wide range of shows featuring ballet, musicals, family shows, drama, concerts, comedy and opera. With a 2100-seater auditorium, the building was designed by Daniel Libeskind and completed in 2010.

voyage.name: The Helix
voyage.address: DCU Glasnevin Campus, Collins Avenue D09 FW22
voyage.content: Event venue and theatre located in the northern suburbs of the city, built in 1996. Hosts a wide variety of talks and performances.

voyage.name: Croke Park Stadium
voyage.content: This stages Gaelic football and hurling for Dublin County GAA and national competitions, with a playing season April-Sep. The stadium has a capacity of 82,300 yet you may struggle to get tickets for big games. Tours of the stadium and GAA museum are also available, including a chance to try out these sports. You can also take the "skyline walk" across the stadium roof.

voyage.name: Leinster Rugby
voyage.address: RDS Arena, Anglesea Rd, Ballsbridge D04 AK83
voyage.content: Leinster play in the United Rugby Championship, the professional European league, and often win it. The stadium has a capacity of 18,500 and big games sometimes transfer to Aviva stadium.

voyage.name: Shamrock Rovers
voyage.address: Tallaght Stadium, Whitestown Way D24 FNK6
voyage.content: They play in the League of Ireland Premier Division, the top tier. The stadium (capacity 10,500) is on N81 two km west of M50.

voyage.name: Leopardstown Racecourse
voyage.content: This has regular meetings throughout the year, flat-racing in summer and jumps in winter. There's a "Pay as you Play" golf course within the racecourse grounds, as well as bars, restaurants and a nightclub.

voyage.name: Irish Film Institute
voyage.address: 6 Eustace Street, Temple Bar D02 PD85
voyage.content: Arthouse cinema for independent Irish and international movies.

voyage.name: Conradh na Gaeilge
voyage.content: Cultural centre where Irish is the first language. They organise events and classes.

voyage.name: Brown Thomas
voyage.content: Dublin's best-known and expensive department store.

voyage.name: Kilkenny Design
voyage.content: Clothing, jewellery and giftware.

voyage.name: Hodges Figgis
voyage.content: Well-stocked large bookshop, part of the Waterstones chain.

voyage.name: Powerscourt Centre
voyage.content: Attractive shopping centre in a beautifully restored 18th-century townhouse, with clothes, cafes, galleries and jewellers. You're paying premium prices for the elegant location.

voyage.name: George's Street Arcade
voyage.content: A covered red-brick shopping arcade, with vintage clothing, fabrics, unusual accessories, vinyl and club wear. It also has some small cafes.

voyage.name: Arnott's
voyage.content: A large department store with a long history.

voyage.name: Jervis Shopping Centre
voyage.content: Shopping centre with some 50 stores.

voyage.name: Ilac Centre
voyage.content: This shopping centre has some 40 stores. The city Central Library is on the first floor.

voyage.name: Chapters Bookstore
voyage.address: Ivy Exchange, Parnell Street D01 P8C2
voyage.content: Huge selection of books at keen prices, as well as a large secondhand section.

voyage.name: Bewley's Café
voyage.content: Grand stylish coffee shop, a Dublin institution. It's had some famous regular customers, from Joyce to Geldof, but they'll make you feel just as important.

voyage.name: Butlers Chocolate Café
voyage.content: Chain of chocolate-themed cafes, Wicklow Street is the original outlet. There are three others in city centre, plus airside in T1 and T2 at the airport. They also ship orders.

voyage.name: Lemon Crèpe & Coffee Company
voyage.content: Good value filled crèpes, they also do waffles and sandwiches.

voyage.name: Govinda's
voyage.content: Hare Krishna-run vegetarian restaurant. Filling portions, only order their Special if you're really hungry.

voyage.name: Pablo Picante
voyage.content: Small friendly Mexican eatery, eat in or take away to nearby St Stephen's Green. They also have outlets at Clarendon Market and Dawson St.

voyage.name: Zaytoon
voyage.content: Casual Persian restaurant. They also have a fast-food cafe in Temple Bar (corner of Parliament St and Essex St).

voyage.name: Bad Ass Café
voyage.content: Modern pub and entertainment venue for US-themed food, plus trad Irish beer and live music.

voyage.name: Balfes
voyage.content: Lively seafood restaurant with outdoor terrace.

voyage.name: Bar Italia
voyage.content: Good value Italian with great atmosphere.

voyage.name: Cornucopia
voyage.content: Smart modern restaurant for vegan and other wholefood options.

voyage.name: Dunne & Crescenzi
voyage.content: Smart trattoria, rightly popular so get there early.

voyage.name: Caketopia
voyage.price: Cakes starting at 70€ serving up to 10 people
voyage.content: Artisan home-made cakes for any occasion for collection or delivery all over Dublin and surrounding areas.

voyage.name: FX Buckley Steakhouse
voyage.content: Quality steaks in a friendly and comfortable restaurant. Plus other meat and seafood, but not much for veggies.

voyage.name: Gallagher's Boxty House
voyage.content: Good traditional Irish fare and not expensive. A boxty is a traditional Irish potato pancake filled and rolled up. Also try the Irish stew and the chowder. Small, friendly, traditional Irish decor.

voyage.name: Elephant & Castle
voyage.content: Famous and popular for its chicken wings, you could have a long wait for a table Saturday lunchtime. It's now a national chain but this is the original outlet.

voyage.name: Peploe's
voyage.content: Excellent basement wine bar and bistro.

voyage.name: Salamanca
voyage.content: Good value, tasty and substantial tapas, sized more like raciones.

voyage.name: TP Smiths
voyage.content: Good pub food, handy if you're shopping around Henry Street.

voyage.name: Bang Restaurant
voyage.hours: Mon–Tue 5–9:30PM, Wed-Fri noon–3PM and 5–9:30PM, Sat 1–4PM and 4–10:30PM
voyage.content: A great cosmopolitan menu. Not cheap, but food and presentation is excellent.

voyage.name: Brasserie Sixty6
voyage.address: 66 South Great Georges Street D02 YD61
voyage.content: Large, stylish modern European restaurant gets good reviews for food, service and atmosphere.

voyage.name: Fire Steakhouse
voyage.address: Mansion House, Dawson Street D02 AF30
voyage.content: Casual dining restaurant in the former Supper Room of the Lord Mayor.

voyage.name: L'Gueuleton
voyage.content: Pricey but highly-rated and popular place.

voyage.name: Kites
voyage.content: Chinese, predominantly Cantonese, also in Szechuan, Peking and Thai style, gets great reviews.

voyage.name: Restaurant Patrick Guilbaud
voyage.content: Expensive but outstanding restaurant.

voyage.name: Roly's Bistro
voyage.content: Lively bistro offering set menus.

voyage.name: Peadar Kearney's
voyage.content: Named for Peadar Ó Cearnaígh (1883-1942) who penned Amhráin na bhFiann, Ireland's national anthem, and was uncle to the three Behans, authors and prolific drinkers all. The pub is a great spot for pre- and post-gig drinks next to Olympia Theatre, with a young crowd and live music from up and coming Irish trad bands. Mostly tourists here but a nice spot to talk to other visitors.

voyage.name: The Cobblestone
voyage.content: They describe themselves as "a drinking pub with a music problem" and have nightly trad sessions.

voyage.name: Frank Ryans
voyage.content: This pub and pizzeria has friendly bar staff and a mixed crowd of students, law types, trendies and locals. Expect weekly trad nights interspersed with Rockabilly, Country and Soul on the jukebox.

voyage.name: O'Donoghue's
voyage.content: With two bars across a courtyard, it's famous for impromptu live music, and where folk group The Dubliners were formed. They have rooms.

voyage.name: The Barge
voyage.content: Friendly trad pub with four areas, good food and great decor.

voyage.name: Hartigan's
voyage.content: Popular student bar, good choice after international rugby matches.

voyage.name: The Brazen Head
voyage.content: Surely the oldest pub in Dublin, founded in 1198 - Ireland's oldest, in Athlone, is from 900 AD. Wonderful on warm, dry summer nights. Live trad music and friendly atmosphere. One of the bars is covered in signed currency notes, there's quite a collection but lacking any bitcoins.

voyage.name: Ned O'Shea's
voyage.content: Decent food and live music and dancing. Ned O’Shea (1937-2018) was a famous trad musician from Kerry.

voyage.name: John Fallon's
voyage.content: Small friendly local pub.

voyage.name: The Oval
voyage.content: Good for drink and food, does an excellent Irish stew. Attracts a mixed age group. Lots of pictures of old Irish celebrities with a tribute to the Quiet Man.

voyage.name: John Kavanagh's
voyage.content: Mournfully authentic pub from 1833 and little altered, where you toast the departed in the next-door cemetery.

voyage.name: Bowe's Lounge Bar
voyage.content: Victorian pub with a huge selection of whiskey.

voyage.name: Mulligans
voyage.content: Busy pub with great Guinness and plenty of history, having been frequented by James Joyce among others.

voyage.name: Nancy Hands
voyage.content: Family-friendly restaurant and bar by entrance to Phoenix Park.

voyage.name: Ryan's
voyage.content: Beautiful Victorian pub, part of Buckley Steakhouse chain. A good place for a pint or meal before getting a train out of Heuston.

voyage.name: Palace Bar
voyage.content: Trad bar with interesting decor complete with "snug" (small private booth). Live music upstairs.

voyage.name: The Long Hall
voyage.address: 31 South Great Georges St D02 DV744
voyage.content: Atmospheric bar with Victorian decor, one of the last "long hall" bars in Ireland.

voyage.name: Kehoe's
voyage.content: An excellent spot for a pint or a meal after a days' sight-seeing or shopping. Several snugs downstairs.

voyage.name: Kennedy's
voyage.content: Trad-style pub serving good food and drink with plenty of friendly atmosphere.

voyage.name: O'Neill's
voyage.content: Excellent atmosphere in a Victorian style pub. They have great food with weekend lunchtime carvery.

voyage.name: The Stag's Head
voyage.content: Trad Victorian pub, no TV, just great ales and conversation.

voyage.name: Dawson Lounge
voyage.content: Probably Dublin's smallest pub - 20 customers and it's packed.

voyage.name: McDaids
voyage.content: This trad pub was a regular place for Brendan Behan and Oscar Wilde to ponder life.

voyage.name: Grogan's
voyage.content: Wonderful trad pub, no music or TV. Great Guinness and a mixture of tourists and locals, with a hotchpotch of interesting art on the walls.

voyage.name: The Bailey
voyage.content: Contemporary bar with tapas, presided over by a portrait of James Joyce. Nice outdoor seating, very busy on summer afternoons and evenings.

voyage.name: The Lotts
voyage.content: Cafe bar, elegant interior with chandeliers, a marble bar and comfortable leather seating. Live music many nights. Small outside seating area.

voyage.name: Market Bar
voyage.content: Spacious bar and tapas restaurant with a good value menu.

voyage.name: The Odeon
voyage.hours: Tue Wed noon-11:30PM, Thu Fri noon-2:30AM, Sat 3PM-2:30AM
voyage.content: This attractive bar at the top of Harcourt St is in a converted railway station.

voyage.name: Pygmalion
voyage.content: Busy bar and restaurant with Med food, best book if you hope to eat.

voyage.name: Café en Seine
voyage.content: Swish megapub on 3 floors, pricey.

voyage.name: Against the Grain
voyage.content: Owned by a Galway brewery, this has a wide variety of Irish micro-brews and world beers. No generic commercial beers on tap. A vibrant pub with an eclectic clientele.

voyage.name: Bull and Castle
voyage.content: Gastropub and beer hall with a large selection of micro-brewed and international beers. Part of Buckley Steakhouse chain.

voyage.name: JR Mahon's
voyage.content: Spread over two stories, they produce a very good stout quite different to Guinness, fresher and more complex, plus their own ale and lager. Also has good cafeteria-style lunch.

voyage.name: Porterhouse
voyage.content: Indigenous brews including an oyster stout, plus an extensive Belgian and international beer list. Also does reasonably priced food. Has sister pubs on Grafton St and in Bray and Phibsboro.

voyage.name: The Foggy Dew
voyage.hours: Mon-Thu noon-midnight, Fri Sat noon-1AM, Sun 2PM-midnight
voyage.address: 1 Fownes Street, Temple Bar D02 WP21
voyage.content: Popular central Victorian-styled pub.

voyage.name: Bruxelles
voyage.content: Lively pub founded in 1886. Spread over 3 bars the music is loud and the atmosphere is buzzing. Outside is a statue of Phil Lynott, from Irish rock band Thin Lizzy. For metal, rock and indie music go downstairs.

voyage.name: The Duke
voyage.content: Great after-work bar and Fridays it's packed to the door.

voyage.name: O'Donoghues
voyage.content: A comfortable bar with live music and TV sport. It's also a hang-out spot for some of the city's most well-known musicians, actors and DJs.

voyage.name: Fibber Magees
voyage.content: A heavy metal bar, handy for Rotunda Hospital.

voyage.name: O'Reillys
voyage.content: Victorian Gothic pub beneath the DART station, with Hell Club Saturday late-night music.

voyage.name: Button Factory
voyage.address: Curved St, Temple Bar D02 RD26
voyage.content: One of Dublin's top clubs and live venues. Main venue has 550 capacity, Crowbar is both a theatre bar and a 60-person venue itself.

voyage.name: The Workmans Club
voyage.content: From 1888 to 2003 this was the city's Working Mens Club, turning into a live entertainment venue in 2010. It's on two floors, the main live room is 300 capacity and beside it is the venue bar. It's friendly, relaxing and well-run.

voyage.name: The Academy
voyage.content: This is primarily a live performance venue, and Friday and Saturday are clubbing nights.

voyage.name: Copper Face Jacks
voyage.content: Legendary club, a post-pub meat-market. Over 20s only, some of the clientele hoping to cop off are going on 120. Rooms available for private events.

voyage.name: The George
voyage.address: 89 South Great George's St D02 R220
voyage.content: The oldest gay bar in Dublin, with late-night drag shows, karaoke, bingo and DJs.

voyage.name: Camac Valley Caravan and Camping Park
voyage.content: Friendly well-run site on bus route to city.

voyage.name: Abbey Court Hostel
voyage.content: Clean well-run hostel just off O'Connell St.

voyage.name: Ashling House
voyage.content: Basic accommodation in leafy Drumcondra. Decent rooms but it's not a B&B.

voyage.name: DCU Summer Rooms
voyage.content: Dublin City University offer spare accommodation to the public all year, with most availability June - September. Their three campuses are Glasnevin, All Hallows in Drumcondra, and St Patrick's in city centre.

voyage.name: Latroupe Jacobs Inn
voyage.content: Nice, clean budget hostel with keycard security. Ensuite shower and bathroom as well as an additional washroom at the end of each hall. The bunks are pods so there's extra privacy.

voyage.name: Lyndon House
voyage.content: Basic but clean B&B near the James Joyce Museum and the Custom House.

voyage.name: Travelodge Dublin City Centre
voyage.content: Reliable chain 3-star, clean and efficient. There are three other Travelodges in the city and one at the airport.

voyage.name: Premier Inn Gloucester Street South
voyage.content: Value-for-money chain hotel. There are three other Premier Inns in the city and one at the airport.

voyage.name: Trinity College
voyage.content: TCD accommodation is available May-Sep in single, double or apartment rooms, some en suite. There is limited access to the campus after midnight, which can result in a long walk from the main gate to some of the residences.

voyage.name: Generator Dublin
voyage.content: Smart hostel. Open social spaces but also a bar and a café to its guests. There are male and female shared rooms that come with all facilities, plus private rooms. Group bookings and private hires available.

voyage.name: Albany House
voyage.content: Good central 3-star, some noise in street-facing rooms. Shower and taps take 5 min to run hot, keep running and have faith.

voyage.name: Ariel House
voyage.content: Comfy welcoming B&B near Aviva stadium. No dogs.

voyage.name: Baggot Court Townhouse
voyage.content: Decent 3-star Georgian townhouse.

voyage.name: Belvedere Hotel
voyage.content: Swish hotel in a Georgian townhouse.

voyage.name: Clayton Hotel Ballsbridge
voyage.content: Splendid hotel in 19th-century school building, 3 km south of centre. They have three other hotels in town and one at the airport.

voyage.name: Buswells Hotel
voyage.content: Cosy Georgian hotel, small rooms but friendly staff, good location.

voyage.name: Castle Hotel
voyage.content: Welcoming Georgian hotel with 130 bedrooms all en suite. Restaurant & bar with live Irish music every weekend.

voyage.name: Dublin Citi Hotel
voyage.address: 46-49 Dame St, Temple Bar D02 X466
voyage.content: Friendly hotel in a busy central spot, all rooms en suite, with Trinity Bar.

voyage.name: Handel's Hotel
voyage.address: 16-18 Fishamble St, Temple Bar D08 E7R0
voyage.content: Central hotel in the west end of Temple Bar, cleaning could be better.

voyage.name: Fitzwilliam Townhouse
voyage.content: Georgian house with many original features. All room en-suite with free Wi-Fi. Decent place, you're paying for the great location.

voyage.name: Fleet Hotel
voyage.address: 19-20 Fleet St, Temple Bar D02 WP97
voyage.content: Central hotel, most rooms comfy, some a bit worn.

voyage.name: Leonardo Hotels
voyage.content: Mid-range chain with two locations: Christchurch, facing Christ Church Cathedral and Temple Bar, and Parnell St, junction with Granby Row.

voyage.name: Maldron Hotel Parnell Square
voyage.content: Clean welcoming hotel, the area is a bit rundown. Maldron have three other hotels in the city and one at the airport.

voyage.name: Morehampton Townhouse
voyage.content: Creaky old building with all 22 room en suite, wi-fi, car parking.

voyage.name: Sandymount Hotel
voyage.content: Slick friendly hotel in Ballsbridge 200 m southeast of Aviva Stadium, sizeable rooms and good bar.

voyage.name: Talbot Hotel Stillorgan
voyage.content: Upmarket hotel with spa, restaurant, bar and free car park.

voyage.name: Clarence Hotel
voyage.content: Owned by Bono and The Edge from Irish band U2, buzzing happening sort of place... code for, you may get a lot of noise from Temple Bar, and "cool" means the showers are a tad lukeish. Overall it's a good central 4-star for 5-star prices: you're paying for the rock associations.

voyage.name: Waterloo Lodge
voyage.content: 3-star in quiet area. All 20 rooms are en-suite, free car parking.

voyage.name: Waterloo Townhouse
voyage.content: Pleasant B&B in a quiet area. No dogs.

voyage.name: Aspect Hotel Parkwest
voyage.content: Edge of city hotel next to Park West & Cherry Orchard railway station and near Exit 9 of M50. Comfy, good service.

voyage.name: Premier Suites Sandyford
voyage.address: Ballymoss Road, Sandyford Industrial Estate D18 DHR0
voyage.content: Serviced apartments available for short stays.

voyage.name: Maldron Hotel Smithfield
voyage.content: Pleasant modern hotel just north of distillery. 92 rooms including family rooms, sleeping up to 6 people.

voyage.name: InterContinental Dublin
voyage.content: Great reviews for comfort and service.

voyage.name: Hampton by Hilton
voyage.content: Boxy modern place in the legal quarter.

voyage.name: Hilton Dublin
voyage.content: Pleasant, modern hotel 1 km south of centre, clean and quiet.

voyage.name: The Morrison
voyage.content: Comfortable stylish hotel, central for sights. Part of Hilton chain.

voyage.name: Radisson Blu Royal Hotel
voyage.content: Business-type hotel in a modern building, swish comfy interior and good location.

voyage.name: Radisson Blu St Helen's Hotel
voyage.content: Upscale hotel in grand old mansion in southern suburbs, on bus route to centre.

voyage.name: The Morgan
voyage.address: 10 Fleet St, Temple Bar D02 AT86
voyage.content: Stylish accommodation in standard rooms, suites or penthouse apartments. All characterised by clean, modern design.

voyage.name: The Shelbourne
voyage.content: Plush hotel overlooking St Stephen's Green, part of the Marriott chain. Fine old building from 1824.

voyage.name: Alex Hotel
voyage.content: Gets great reviews for comfort and dining.

voyage.name: Spencer Hotel
voyage.content: Chic, luxurious five-star hotel in the docklands. The quay outside is busy, rooms at the back are quieter.

voyage.name: Mont Hotel
voyage.content: Slick central hotel, some street noise.

voyage.name: Green Hotel
voyage.content: Comfy spacious hotel at the west corner of St Stephen's Green.

voyage.name: Davenport Hotel
voyage.content: Great reviews for this elegant hotel at the heart of Georgian Dublin.

voyage.name: The Leinster
voyage.content: Ugly boxy modern building, but great reviews for comfort and service.

voyage.name: Maldron Hotel
voyage.address: Corballis Way, Dublin Airport K67 T6P6
voyage.content: Mid-price hotel opposite Radisson Blu.

voyage.name: Radisson Blu Hotel Dublin Airport
voyage.address: Corballis Way, Dublin Airport K67 H5H9
voyage.content: Comfy accommodation within the airport complex just minutes from the passenger terminals.

voyage.name: Clayton Hotel Dublin Airport
voyage.content: Convenient mid-range hotel with free shuttle to the airport.

voyage.name: Carlton Hotel
voyage.address: Old Airport Rd, Cloghran K67 P5C7
voyage.content: Mid-price hotel with free shuttle to the airport. Bar-food menu and a restaurant on the top floor.
